This makes the roles clear. The estimator decides how observations represent the target image. The controller decides where another observation is worth its cost. A controller may use a bandit to learn which region tends to yield more error reduction per unit time, while the final pixel estimate still uses area-correct weights. If reward is defined as immediate reduction in a perceptual loss, however, that reward may be noisy, nonstationary, and dependent on prior denoising state. UCB's guarantee is about maximizing cumulative expected reward under its bandit model; it does not imply a radiometrically unbiased image, a calibrated pixelwise interval, or a globally optimal perceptual image.

The same separation applies in vision. If a system selects uncertain image patches for labeling, it can use the resulting data to improve a classifier, but naïvely averaging only the selected labels estimates the selected-patch distribution. Population-level metrics require either representative sampling, known inclusion probabilities with valid weights, or a justified model-based adjustment. If an engine prioritizes collision checks near suspected contacts, the hit rate among queried pairs is not the scene-wide collision rate. Active computation can improve decisions while making naïve descriptive summaries less representative.

A final nuance is that a reward itself can be estimated. Suppose action A costs 1 ms and reduces estimated error by $0.02$ with high variance, while action B costs 3 ms and reduces it by $0.05$ with low variance. “Maximize error reduction” selects B by mean reward; “maximize reduction per millisecond” may select A; “minimize error subject to a frame-time cap” is a constrained objective. If actions alter caches or future variance, their reward depends on history and may not be stationary. Naming the utility and horizon is part of the scientific model, not a presentation detail.

For reproducibility, preserve at least a replayable trace of chosen actions, conditional selection probabilities, reward observations, sample counts, stopping times, and estimator weights. With this trace, one can separately check the controller's decisions and recompute the estimator. A seed alone cannot reveal whether support was missing, whether confidence was repeatedly checked, or whether a renderer's next sample distribution depended on a previous noisy estimate.

## Numerical integration and Monte Carlo estimation

Numerical integration approximates transport quantities, and sampling choices determine bias, variance, and convergence.

### Variance reduction for rendering

Variance is the spread of estimates around their expected value. Bias is systematic error in that expectation. Consistency means estimates approach the target as sample count grows. An unbiased method can look noisy; a visually smooth method can be biased. Clamping rare bright samples may reduce visible fireflies but changes the expected image. The right question is both what result the method converges to and how quickly it converges. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Uniform hemisphere sampling often misses a small bright light. Importance sampling chooses the light’s solid angle more frequently and divides by its density. BSDF sampling chooses directions favored by the material. [[Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance|Multiple importance sampling]] combines both strategies with weights that sum to one, so a strategy that rarely finds a contribution is not trusted disproportionately. Bidirectional path tracing grows paths from light and camera and joins them. Metropolis light transport mutates high-contribution paths to explore nearby regions. These techniques target rare or important light paths that naive sampling may miss. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Sample patterns change the spectrum of error. Stratified sampling divides the domain into cells and ensures each cell is represented. Low-discrepancy sequences spread points evenly in low dimensions. Blue-noise patterns avoid large clumps without a periodic grid. Poisson-disk sampling enforces minimum separation. CDF sampling maps uniform random numbers to an arbitrary distribution; alias tables accelerate repeated draws from discrete weights. Photon mapping stores light paths for local density estimation, while finite-element radiosity discretizes energy exchange among surface patches. Each method has different memory, bias, and convergence tradeoffs. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

The function being integrated has its own variance; a sampling method cannot change that function. What the renderer can change is the variance of its estimator: the randomness in the numerical answer across repeated runs or samples. This distinction is visible with a checkerboard function that is 0 on black cells and 1 on white cells. Over equal black and white area, its mean is $1/2$ and its variance is $1/4$. That variance belongs to the integrand. A different estimator can reduce uncertainty in the integral by guaranteeing representation of both cell colors. It cannot make the checkerboard itself less variable. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Bias and consistency are separate tests. An estimator is unbiased when its expected result equals the true integral at a fixed sample count. It is consistent when the probability of a fixed-sized error tends toward zero as sample count grows. A fixed grid that is refined into smaller cells can converge to an image integral and thus be consistent, yet the grid estimate at any finite resolution is not a random variable centered on the exact answer. Conversely, picking one uniformly random image point and multiplying its color by image area is unbiased: averaging that estimator over many repeated trials gives the integral. But if the procedure permanently uses just one point, its estimate does not converge as its sample budget increases because it has no increasing budget. Standard Monte Carlo with more independent points is both. This vocabulary matters because consistency says the method can get there, while unbiasedness says it is centered correctly before it gets there. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Importance sampling has an ideal limit that explains why matching the proposal to the integrand helps. For a nonnegative integrand $f(x)$ with integral $I$, the density $p(x)=f(x)/I$ makes every weighted sample $f(X)/p(X)$ equal to $I$. One sample would then suffice. But constructing that density requires knowing $I$, the unknown answer, so it is a useful ideal rather than a practical recipe. Rendering uses approximations: sample a glossy material near its reflected direction, use cosine weighting for diffuse response, or sample a point light exactly rather than hope a random hemisphere ray finds it. Area-light sampling and material sampling can succeed in different cases. Multiple importance sampling (MIS) combines them. With two proposal densities $p_1,p_2$, and fractions $n_1/N,n_2/N$ of the total samples, the balance heuristic divides a sample's integrand value by the combined density $(n_1/N)p_1(x)+(n_2/N)p_2(x)$. Contributions from both strategies then estimate the same integral without trusting a strategy that rarely reaches an important region. A scene grid spanning point-to-area lights and near-mirror-to-diffuse materials demonstrates why neither light-only nor material-only sampling is uniformly best. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Some lighting paths are so narrow that ordinary eye-originating path tracing almost never finds them. In a glossy coffee-cup example, a bright source reflects from the curved cup and forms a caustic ring on a diffuse table. A path from the eye to the table to the mirror-like cup to a point source is valid, but after a random diffuse bounce the exact direction needed at a perfect mirror has zero probability under a continuous directional distribution; the subsequent point source also occupies zero solid angle. A real light and surface may be merely small and glossy rather than mathematical deltas, yet the same path may remain extremely rare. A disco-ball scene makes the compounding difficulty visible: a camera ray must find a tiny bright region on a wall, then a tiny region of the mirrored ball that reflects the source. Raising samples from 16 to 128 to 8,192 eventually reveals the caustic, but this spends work on paths that carry almost no light. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Bidirectional path tracing samples partial paths from both ends. One subpath starts at the camera; another starts at a light. Connecting their endpoints can find transport arrangements that either one-sided strategy misses, such as a path that must reach a point source or a pinhole camera. Each connection needs a weight based on the probability of producing that same full path under the competing sampling strategies. Different combinations of camera-side and light-side path lengths reveal different effects; a glass egg may show its transmitted illumination for a particular split even when neighboring splits do not. Bidirectional tracing still has geometric failures: if the only path passes through a barely open door, most sampled endpoints connect through a wall and contribute zero. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Metropolis light transport addresses rare but high-value regions by sampling dependent paths. From current path $x$, propose path $y$ with transition density $T(y\mid x)$ and accept it with probability

$$
\alpha(x,y)=\min\!\left(1,\frac{\pi(y)T(x\mid y)}{\pi(x)T(y\mid x)}\right),
$$

 where $\pi$ is the target path-contribution density. For symmetric proposals, the transition-density factors cancel, leaving the capped ratio of new to old target density; for an asymmetric proposal, omitting these factors biases the chain. Rejected proposals retain the current path. Repeated states spend more samples in high-contribution regions. This is a Markov chain, so consecutive samples are dependent; the mutation must be able to reach every relevant region (ergodicity), and an initial transient must not be mistaken for the target distribution. Gaussian local mutations with occasional global proposals can help the chain escape isolated regions, provided the proposal probabilities are included in $T$. The lecture illustrates the idea by walking over an image: visit bright pixels more often and accumulated counts reconstruct downtown Pittsburgh; in rendering, mutate a discovered bright light path to find nearby bright paths. This can lower variance for caustics such as light refracting into and out of a swimming pool, at the cost of chain setup and correlation. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Sampling layout matters in addition to the probability density. Purely random points are uniform in distribution but can clump and leave large holes in a finite realization. Stratification divides the domain into $N$ bins and draws one random point in each. It keeps each region represented, and cannot have larger variance than the corresponding unstratified estimator under the stated partition because each bin's contribution is estimated separately. This works on intervals, image pixels, or a projected light patch on a hemisphere. Low-discrepancy samples instead try to make the fraction of points in each region match its area. Their discrepancy measures the worst mismatch over a chosen family of regions. Koksma's theorem relates integration error to sample discrepancy times the total variation of the integrand; discontinuities make this bound loose or infinite for some rendering integrands, so it is guidance rather than a blanket guarantee. Halton points use radical inverses: write an integer in a base and reflect its digits across the decimal point, using different prime bases for dimensions. Hammersley sequences add a coordinate $i/N$ and the remaining radical-inverse coordinates; they often look more even, but require knowing $N$ in advance. Regular grids have low discrepancy for many boxes yet can alias badly: shifting a grid relative to a sinusoid can change an average from nearly one to nearly zero. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Blue-noise sample patterns seek good spatial and frequency behavior together. A pattern with no preferred direction is isotropic; one without strong periodic peaks avoids locking to features of a particular scale. In a Fourier spectrum, radius represents spatial frequency and angle represents direction. A square grid has strong spectral peaks at frequencies aligned with its axes. A blue-noise pattern has a ring associated with minimum point separation, while higher frequencies are more evenly represented. This helps a high-frequency zone-plate image average toward gray without visible directional bands, though no finite sample set eliminates every artifact. Poisson-disk sampling enforces a minimum distance by rejecting new points whose disks overlap existing samples. Lloyd relaxation moves sites toward centroids of their Voronoi cells, the regions closest to each site, and can produce an even more regular pattern; weighted cells allocate more samples to bright regions in an environment map. These methods cost preprocessing but can pay off when a sample pattern is reused across many pixels or frames. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Large discrete distributions also need an efficient sampler. A cumulative distribution function (CDF) stores cumulative event weights; binary search draws one event in $O(\log n)$ time after preprocessing. An alias table transforms the distribution into $n$ equal-width columns, each containing at most two event labels and a threshold. Sampling chooses a column uniformly and makes one threshold comparison to select its primary or alias event, giving $O(1)$ work per draw after setup. This is useful for repeated environment-map sampling. Two other global-illumination methods illustrate different tradeoffs: photon mapping traces energy from lights and stores photon hits in a spatial structure such as a $k$-d tree, then gathers nearby photons at eye-visible points, which is effective for caustics and participating media but biased at finite photon radius/count; finite-element radiosity divides diffuse surfaces into patches and solves a linear system for equilibrium exchange, but cannot represent general glossy transport and needs suitable mesh elements. No finite sampling strategy can certify that an unseen bright path does not exist: an arbitrarily tiny opening can connect a dark camera room to an arbitrarily bright source. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Russian roulette terminates paths randomly rather than truncating every path at the same bounce. If a contribution $C$ continues with probability $q$, a surviving path carries $C/q$. Expected contribution remains $q(C/q)+(1-q)0=C$, preserving expectation while reducing work. Too small a continuation probability creates large weights and can increase variance. [[#CMU-18 - Monte Carlo Rendering|CMU-18]] · [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

### Error of quadrature

For a smooth function, midpoint and trapezoidal rules become more accurate as intervals shrink. Midpoint’s leading error depends on second derivative; Simpson’s rule uses pairs of intervals and a quadratic approximation, giving higher order accuracy when the function is sufficiently smooth. However, a visibility function can jump from 0 to 1 at a silhouette, and glossy reflections create narrow peaks. Smoothness assumptions matter. More quadrature samples in a uniform grid may waste most work away from a narrow peak.

In multiple dimensions, tensor-product grids grow exponentially. With $m$ positions along each of $d$ axes, the number of evaluations is $m^d$. Monte Carlo’s standard error depends roughly on $1/\sqrt{N}$ regardless of dimension under broad conditions, making it useful for high-dimensional paths. Quasi-Monte Carlo sequences can exploit low-dimensional regularity to improve convergence, but arbitrary high-dimensional integrands and discontinuities can reduce the advantage. The numerical method should match the domain structure. [[#CMU-17 - Numerical Integration|CMU-17]] · [[#CMU-18 - Monte Carlo Rendering|CMU-18]] · [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

### Importance sampling and support

Sampling density $p(x)$ must have support everywhere the integrand contributes. If $p(x)=0$ where $f(x)\ne0$, the estimator cannot see that contribution and becomes biased. If $p$ is tiny where $f$ is large, a rare sample receives a huge weight $f/p$, producing high variance. Choosing $p$ proportional to $|f|$ is ideal for a nonnegative known integrand, but renderers only approximate it because full integrand values include unknown visibility and future bounces.

A cosine-weighted hemisphere sampler chooses directions with density $p(\omega)=\cos\theta/\pi$. Since Lambertian BRDF includes a cosine factor, the sample weight simplifies and variance drops relative to uniform directions. A light sampler instead chooses points on emitters, with area density converted to solid-angle density using distance and light-normal cosine. These two samplers are complementary. [[#CMU-18 - Monte Carlo Rendering|CMU-18]] · [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Multiple importance sampling with two techniques uses a weight such as

$$
w_j(x)=\frac{n_jp_j(x)}{n_1p_1(x)+n_2p_2(x)},
$$

where $p_j$ is technique $j$’s density and $n_j$ its sample count. The weights sum to one. If a light-sampled direction is unlikely under the BSDF sampler but likely under the light sampler, the light technique receives most of the weight. If a direction lies under both distributions, they share the contribution. This avoids choosing one strategy that performs well for one material-light configuration and poorly for another. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

### Variance is visible as image noise

For random variable $Y$, variance is $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb E[(Y-\mathbb E[Y])^2]$. The sample mean of $N$ independent observations has variance $\operatorname{Var}(Y)/N$. An image estimator produces one such random estimate per pixel; neighboring estimates may be correlated if they share samples or paths. Noise appears as spatially varying error. A more efficient estimator reduces variance per unit computation, not only variance per sample.

Stratification reduces the chance that a whole part of the domain receives no sample. Low-discrepancy point sets reduce large-scale holes. Blue-noise distributions avoid both clumping and periodic structure. Importance sampling places samples based on expected contribution. MIS combines samplers. Russian roulette trades variable work for unbiased termination. Denoising can reduce visible noise by exploiting image structure, but if it changes the expected signal, it introduces bias. The design question is where the estimator’s error goes and what assumptions are used to suppress it. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

### Sampling a nonuniform probability distribution

Suppose a toy density on $[0,1]$ is $p(x)=3(1-x)^2$. Its cumulative distribution is

$$
F(x)=\int_0^x3(1-t)^2dt=1-(1-x)^3.
$$

Given uniform random number $U\in[0,1]$, set $U=F(x)$ and invert: $x=1-(1-U)^{1/3}$. Values concentrate near zero where density is higher. This inverse-CDF method transforms uniform random bits into samples from the target distribution. It also shows that a sampling method is a [[Probability density and change of measure|change of variables]]: the density and Jacobian must be accounted for when estimating an integral. [[#CMU-17 - Numerical Integration|CMU-17]]

### Bias and consistency in image estimators

An estimator that takes a fixed regular grid of $m\times m$ image samples and sums them can converge to the correct area integral as the grid is refined, yet a fixed coarse grid may systematically miss a thin feature. It is consistent in the limit but not an unbiased random estimate for one finite random draw. Conversely, choosing one random pixel sample and multiplying by image area is unbiased for the integral, but its variance may be high and it never becomes more informative if the sample count stays at one. These examples separate asymptotic convergence from finite-sample correctness. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

Point lights and perfect mirrors form a pathological case for some path-sampling strategies: important paths occupy an extremely small or zero-measure subset of direction space. A continuous random direction almost surely misses the exact mirror direction. Real systems approximate ideal sources and materials with finite distributions, but can still have sharp peaks. Better sampling, bidirectional path construction, or explicit handling of delta events is needed. [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

### A sample-count budget comparison

Suppose a pixel estimate has standard deviation $\sigma=0.2$ with 100 independent samples. Its expected standard error is $0.2/\sqrt{100}=0.02$. To reach 0.01 with the same estimator, use about 400 samples. If importance sampling reduces per-sample standard deviation from 0.2 to 0.1, 100 samples give standard error 0.01. This comparison shows why algorithmic variance reduction can be more valuable than simply increasing sample count. It also shows the limit: the square-root law is gradual, so halving error by brute force quadruples work. [[#CMU-18 - Monte Carlo Rendering|CMU-18]] · [[#CMU-19 - Variance Reduction|CMU-19]]

### Reservoir resampling for direct-light estimates

*Connect to:* the rendering equation and light transport; Monte Carlo integration; importance sampling; temporal accumulation and visibility.

Direct illumination at a surface point can be written as an integral over the light-emitting surfaces. For a light point $x$ and shading point $y$, the integrand contains the surface response (the BSDF), emitted radiance, a geometry term with distance and cosine factors, and visibility:

$$L(y,\omega)=\int_A \rho(y,\overrightarrow{yx}\leftrightarrow\omega)\,L_e(x\to y)\,G(x\leftrightarrow y)\,V(x\leftrightarrow y)\,dA_x.$$

The hard part is that a sample can be bright before visibility and contribute nothing after a shadow ray finds an occluder. In a scene with thousands of lights, tracing a visibility ray to every source is too expensive. Importance sampling tries to draw more often from parts of the integral that matter. If a proposal density is $p(x)$, a Monte Carlo estimate is

$$\widehat L=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{f(x_i)}{p(x_i)},\qquad x_i\sim p.$$

The proposal must be nonzero wherever the integrand can be nonzero. A proposal that tracks the integrand well tends to reduce variance, but the ideal proposal includes visibility, which is costly to know before tracing the ray.

**Resampled importance sampling (RIS)** uses an easy proposal $p$ to generate a pool of $M$ candidates. Each candidate receives weight $w_i=\widehat p(x_i)/p(x_i)$, where $\widehat p$ approximates the target distribution. Pick one candidate with probability $w_i/\sum_jw_j$. The estimator is

$$\widehat L_{RIS}=\frac{f(y)}{\widehat p(y)}\left(\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^M\frac{\widehat p(x_j)}{p(x_j)}\right).$$

The selected sample $y$ is more likely to come from important regions. The average-weight term corrects for the fact that the selected sample only approximates the target distribution. With a valid proposal and target support, this estimator is unbiased: its expected value equals the integral, even though an individual frame may be noisy.

A **weighted reservoir** stores just one selected sample, the running sum of weights, and the number of candidates. For each new candidate, add its weight to the total and replace the stored sample with probability $w_i/w_{sum}$. After processing any prefix of the stream, each candidate has probability proportional to its weight of being the stored sample. This gives a compact implementation: memory does not grow with the candidate count, although generating and weighting candidates still costs work proportional to $M$.

The key reuse trick follows from the reservoir's state. To merge reservoirs, treat each reservoir's selected sample as one new candidate with weight equal to its accumulated weight. The resulting reservoir is equivalent to processing all original candidate streams together, even though those streams were discarded. Thus one pixel can reuse a sample selected for a neighboring pixel using only compact reservoir records. Repeating this across $k$ neighbors and $n$ rounds lets each pixel benefit from roughly $knM$ original proposals while the reuse work scales like $O(nk+M)$ per pixel.

Temporal reuse carries the final reservoir from a previous frame to a reprojected pixel in the current frame. Motion vectors estimate where the same surface point moved. Spatial reuse combines reservoirs from nearby pixels. Visibility reuse tests the chosen sample before sharing it; discarding an occluded sample can prevent its propagation across a local region. These operations exploit correlation between nearby pixels: adjacent points often have similar lighting and material response, so a useful light sample for one may be useful for another.

There is a catch: adjacent pixels do not necessarily have the same sampling distribution or even the same valid sample domain. A sample below one pixel's surface hemisphere can have zero probability there but be valid at its neighbor. An occluded sample may be discarded at one location but visible at another. If the standard RIS correction assumes every proposal distribution covers the whole target support, reusing samples with different support silently drops valid contributions and darkens the result.

The paper derives the problem explicitly. Let $p_i(x)$ be the proposal distribution that produced candidate $i$, and define $Z(y)=\{i:p_i(y)>0\}$. Under the standard mixed-candidate RIS weight, the conditional expected weight for output $y$ is

$$\mathbb{E}[W\mid y]=\frac{1}{p(y)}\frac{|Z(y)|}{M}.$$

If every candidate distribution is positive wherever the target is positive, then $|Z(y)|=M$ and the correction is right. If only some distributions support $y$, the factor is smaller than one, so the estimate is biased dark. A seemingly simple fix is to divide by the count of supporting distributions. That restores the expected value, but can have enormous variance when a proposal is nonzero yet extremely small in part of the domain.

Instead, the authors assign each proposal a mixture weight using the balance heuristic:

$$m_i(y)=\frac{p_i(y)}{\sum_j p_j(y)}.$$

These weights sum to one wherever the mixture has support, and they downweight proposals that are numerically tiny rather than treating every nonzero proposal equally. The unbiased reservoir-combination procedure must evaluate whether a reused sample is supported at each candidate's source pixel. When visibility forms part of that support test, checking it can require extra shadow rays. This is why the method includes both variants: the cheaper **biased** algorithm heuristically rejects neighbors with different depth or normal and accepts some darkening; the **unbiased** algorithm spends more time to evaluate support correctly.

The paper's implementation begins with 32 light candidates per pixel, samples emissive triangles by power and samples any environment map for 25% of candidates. It uses five random spatial neighbors within a 30-pixel radius, two spatial passes, and reprojects the previous frame for temporal reuse. The unbiased variant uses three neighbors and one spatial pass to keep cost comparable. The biased variant stores four reservoirs per pixel; temporal reservoir count is clamped so old history cannot grow without bound. These values describe the tested renderer, not universal defaults.

**Published evidence and limits.** The authors tested in Falcor on an RTX 2080 Ti (Titan RTX for their largest Amusement Park scene), with thousands to millions of emissive triangles. Against their high-sample reference, the paper reports one to two orders of magnitude lower error at comparable rendering budgets. On interactive budgets, the biased version generally has lower variance but visibly loses energy near shadow boundaries, highlights, and complex geometry. At longer render times, bias dominates and the unbiased version can become more accurate. Reuse is weakest at disocclusions, lighting boundaries, rapidly moving lights, and complex geometry. The original method targets direct lighting at the primary camera-hit surface; it does not automatically solve reuse for arbitrary multi-bounce paths. It is an algorithm for sampling contributions inside the renderer, not a post-process that averages final pixel colors.

**Source:** Bitterli et al., “Spatiotemporal [[Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR|Reservoir Resampling]] for Real-Time Ray Tracing with Dynamic Direct Lighting” (2020), full paper and appendices A–B, PDF pp. 1–17. [Primary PDF](https://benedikt-bitterli.me/restir/bitterli20restir.pdf).

### Reuse paths across geometry LoD changes

*Connect to:* multiscale geometry and level of detail; Monte Carlo path tracing; ReSTIR reservoirs; UV parameterization; temporal reprojection.

A distant object often needs a simpler mesh than a nearby one. A **level of detail (LoD)** is one of several representations of the same object, chosen according to viewing scale. LoD reduces geometric cost and can reduce subpixel detail that would otherwise cause aliasing and noisy path-tracing estimates. But changing LoD changes mesh topology. A temporal path-reuse method that identifies a surface point by triangle ID and barycentric coordinates then fails: triangle 240 on one mesh is not necessarily the same surface location as triangle 240 on another.

Real-Time Level-of-Detail Rendering with ReSTIR replaces that assumption with an explicit vertex map $\tau$ between surface points on two LoD meshes. The authors assume the meshes share a consistent UV texture space. With a non-overlapping UV map $\Phi_1$ on the source and $\Phi_2$ on the target, map a surface point by preserving its UV coordinate:

$$\tau(\mathbf{x})=\Phi_2^{-1}(\Phi_1(\mathbf{x})).$$

This uses the UV parameterization as a common address for corresponding locations. It does not require the two meshes to share vertices, triangle counts, or topology.

UV coordinates can overlap, however. A UV value may refer to several world-space points, such as the same texture reused on both sides of a symmetric object. A shift mapping used by ReSTIR needs a one-to-one correspondence over the points it reuses. The paper collects all surface points from each LoD that share a UV coordinate, then forms a partial matching. Its practical algorithm repeatedly pairs the closest unmatched points in world space and removes both from further matching. Unmatched points have no mapping, so reuse can fail for them. This is safer than treating one UV coordinate as a unique world point when it is not.

The mapping changes area and therefore sample density. Let $q=(u,v)$ be a UV coordinate, and let $\Phi_k^{-1}$ map UV coordinates to surface $S_k$, for $k\in\{1,2\}$. Define $\bar{\mathbf{u}}_k=\partial\Phi_k^{-1}/\partial u$ and $\bar{\mathbf{v}}_k=\partial\Phi_k^{-1}/\partial v$; these tangent vectors give world-space displacement per unit change in each UV coordinate. The surface-area Jacobian is

$$\left|\det\frac{\partial\tau}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\right|=\frac{|\bar{\mathbf{u}}_2\times\bar{\mathbf{v}}_2|}{|\bar{\mathbf{u}}_1\times\bar{\mathbf{v}}_1|}.$$

$$\left|\det\frac{\partial\tau}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\right|=\frac{|\bar{\mathbf{u}}_2\times\bar{\mathbf{v}}_2|}{|\bar{\mathbf{u}}_1\times\bar{\mathbf{v}}_1|}.$$

This ratio compares the world-space area represented by the same small UV patch on the two meshes. It multiplies the usual shift-mapping Jacobian for each mapped path vertex. Without this correction, a path could be over- or under-counted simply because one LoD allocates more surface area to that UV region.

In path reuse, a path has several vertices: the first surface hit, later scattering points, and a reconnection vertex where a shifted path rejoins the sampled path. During temporal reuse, 3DGUT-LOD first maps the previous frame's primary hit with $\tau$ and reprojects it into the current image. It then applies the existing hybrid shift to the rest of the path and uses $\tau$ for the reconnection vertex. The mapping data needed by the shift are stored in the path reservoir: object identity and UV coordinates for the primary hit and reconnection vertex. The Jacobian correction includes $|\partial\tau/\partial\mathbf{x}_i|$ for every vertex mapped across LoD. The paper finds that mapping only the primary hit or only the reconnection point increases noise; both roles need the LoD-aware correspondence.

Spatial reuse is simpler in their setup because every ray in one frame sees the same LoD for an object. The challenging transition occurs between frames. The authors implement the method in Falcor, render at 1920×1080 on an RTX 3090 with an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X, and compare against path tracing and reservoir splatting without the new mapping. Their tests include a rock with animated focus and four LoDs, Sponza statues, terrain, chess pieces, and a coastal cliff. At a LoD switch, ordinary reservoir splatting loses temporal history and becomes noisy; the new mapping allows reuse to continue with a smaller, brief quality loss. Path tracing has no reuse and remains noisier at the same time budget. The paper also tests mirrored and overlapping UVs; the one-to-one matching restores reuse where a naive UV inverse would give up.

**Limits.** This method depends on UV parameterizations that correspond across LoDs. Missing, inconsistent, heavily distorted, or degenerate UV maps can break the surface correspondence or lower image quality. The greedy world-space pairing is a practical matching heuristic, not a proof of semantic correspondence for arbitrary remeshes. Their implementation switches one LoD per object per frame; it does not choose a different LoD for every ray within one frame. The source demonstrates image-space sample reuse across mesh-topology changes, not a general guarantee that all coarse meshes preserve the same physical surface or material detail.

**Source:** Wang et al., “Real-Time Level-of-Detail Rendering with ReSTIR” (SIGGRAPH 2026), complete paper, PDF pp. 1–8. [Primary PDF](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/rtr/publication/wang2026levelOfDetail/wang2026levelOfDetail.pdf).

#### What the companion presentations add

The captioned 3D Gaussian Splatting presentation adds an accessible overview of the paper's pipeline: initialize from a structure-from-motion point cloud, optimize anisotropic Gaussians, and render the scene. It highlights that elongated splats can represent thin structures such as bicycle spokes. It also reports more than 100 frames per second in shown scenes, a 7,000-iteration run taking about six minutes, and an ablation using random rather than structure-from-motion initialization. These are claims made in the presentation and depend on its test setup; the paper's experiments remain the detailed evidence. [Presentation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T_kXY43VZnk).

The 2D Gaussian Splatting presentation foregrounds the reason for a planar primitive: its normal is geometrically meaningful. It also walks through perspective-correct ray/disc intersection, a low-pass filter for small or oblique splats, ray-wise depth concentration, normal consistency, and depth-based mesh extraction. The automatic captions are imperfect, so the paper and its supplement carry the formal definitions and equations. [Presentation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oaHCtB6yiKU).

The Instant Field-Aligned Meshes presentation shows the method as two coupled fields: an orientation field guides edge direction and a position field controls vertex placement. It briefly demonstrates feature alignment, point-cloud input, interactive orientation/position brushes, and very large remeshing. Its claim of processing a 372-million-triangle mesh in about nine minutes is a reported demo result, not an independent benchmark. [Presentation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U6wtw6W4x3I).

### Figure U14 - A reservoir selects a candidate by its weight

![[Visual Recall/University Graphics and Vision/reservoir-selection.png]]

*The conditional selection probabilities match the displayed candidate weights. The picture explains reservoir selection only; correct lighting estimates also require the method normalization and support assumptions.*

## Rasterization, coverage, and depth

## Decide which samples a triangle owns

A pixel is an image location. A sample is a position at which we test coverage or evaluate an image contribution. A fragment is candidate raster work produced by a primitive; tests can discard it, and blending can combine its result with an older value. These words describe different stages. The distinction explains why drawing two triangles can create more fragments than final pixels, and why a covered sample need not cause a stored color change. The Vulkan specification defines raster coverage in terms of sample locations. [Khronos rasterization specification](https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/primsrast.html)

Start with the panel's triangle vertices. The vertex shader produces homogeneous clip coordinates $(x_c,y_c,z_c,w_c)$. Homogeneous means that coordinates carry a common scale: the eventual three-dimensional coordinate is obtained by dividing by $w_c$. Clip against the chosen volume before that division. An edge crossing $w_c=0$ would otherwise produce unbounded screen coordinates. For the usual Vulkan depth convention, the six clip inequalities include $0\le z_c\le w_c$; an alternative depth convention requires corresponding changes.

After clipping and projection, an edge function answers which side of each triangle edge contains a sample. For $A=(x_A,y_A)$, $B=(x_B,y_B)$ and sample $P=(x,y)$, choose

$$
E_{AB}(P)=(x_B-x_A)(y-y_A)-(y_B-y_A)(x-x_A).
$$

The sign is an orientation test. If a triangle is counterclockwise in this coordinate system, its interior lies on the nonnegative side of all three directed edges. A shared edge needs a consistent inclusion rule: otherwise adjacent triangles can both own a boundary sample or neither can own it. A top-left rule is one such tie-breaking convention. Its exact sign test depends on whether screen $y$ increases upward or downward. Do not transplant a code condition without that convention.

The same edge functions produce barycentric coordinates, which are weights describing position inside the triangle. For $A=(0,0)$, $B=(4,0)$, $C=(0,4)$ and $P=(1,1)$, the weights are $(1/2,1/4,1/4)$. They sum to one and reconstruct $P$. This is why coverage and interpolation share arithmetic.

Projection changes these weights. An attribute that varies linearly across the original triangle must be reconstructed using

$$
a(P)=\frac{\sum_i\lambda_i a_i/w_i}{\sum_i\lambda_i/w_i},
$$

where $\lambda_i$ are screen barycentrics and $w_i$ are the vertex clip coordinates. With two endpoints $u=(0,1)$ and $w=(1,4)$, the screen midpoint has $u=0.2$, not $0.5$. The division is the reason a checkerboard stays attached to a receding panel rather than sliding across it.

**Depth has a different interpolation contract.** The normalized depth values $z_{c,i}/w_i$ interpolate affinely in screen barycentrics. Do not take those already-divided depth values and apply the generic attribute formula a second time. Recovering camera distance from the stored depth is a separate inverse-projection operation. This distinction prevents a subtle software-rasterizer bug.

### Give depth an explicit meaning

Let $d>0$ be camera-axis distance, with near plane $n$ and far plane $f$. Conventional zero-to-one depth is

$$
z(d)=\frac{f}{f-n}-\frac{fn}{(f-n)d}.
$$

This maps $n$ to zero and $f$ to one. It does not store distance in metres. [[Concepts/Reversed-Z depth contracts|Reversed depth]] stores $1-z(d)$; with an infinite far plane it becomes $n/d$. Floating-point values become more closely spaced near zero, which pairs usefully with the reciprocal-distance mapping. Reversing a uniformly spaced fixed-point buffer alone does not create more precision. [Nathan Reed's depth precision analysis](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/visualizing-depth-precision/)

For a reversed camera depth path, clear to zero and use the intended greater-depth comparison. A conservative occlusion pyramid then usually stores a region's minimum depth, rather than the maximum used in the corresponding conventional-depth construction. Empty samples, projected bounds crossing the near plane, and equality rules must remain conservative. An object should be culled only when the bound proves that every candidate sample fails; an uncertain bound must remain visible.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Vertex bytes and formats"] --> B["Transform and clip"] --> C["Divide and viewport"] --> D["Coverage and interpolation"] --> E["Tests and shading"] --> F["Blend and store"]
  classDef data fill:#e7f0ff,stroke:#3564a3,color:#16304f;
  classDef work fill:#e8f5ed,stroke:#397951,color:#173d25;
  class A,F data;
  class B,C,D,E work;
```

Read this diagram as a logical dependency chain. Hardware can overlap, combine, or move work where API rules permit it. It is not a promise that every GPU executes these boxes as six separate serial units.

Implementation-specific passages retain observations from the supplied Kairo/Maveb snapshot. They are not a fresh audit of those repositories. Source exercises and illustrative code are teaching material; only explicitly recorded checks have been executed here.


**SYSTEM QUESTION:** How does a GPU take a few indexed 3D vertices and deterministically decide **which framebuffer samples belong to which triangle, what values exist at those samples, and whether those samples survive depth testing?**

The original contract gives the exact chain: rasterization motivation → vertex/index records → topology and assembly → shader invocation → input layouts → MVP → clip position → homogeneous clipping → perspective division → NDC → viewport → triangle setup → edge functions → coverage → barycentrics → perspective interpolation → fragment derivatives → early/late depth → precision → reversed-Z.

---

**What rasterization is actually solving**

Suppose a triangle exists mathematically in continuous 3D space.

Its vertices might be

$$
P_0=(-1,-1,-5),\qquad
P_1=(1,-1,-5),\qquad
P_2=(0,1,-5).
$$

Your display, however, is not continuous. It might be a grid such as

$$
1920\times1080
$$

containing discrete pixel locations, and potentially several **samples per pixel** if multisampling is enabled.

There is therefore a fundamental conversion:

$$
\boxed{\text{continuous geometric primitive}
\longrightarrow
\text{discrete covered samples}}
$$

That conversion is rasterization.

A rasterizer does **not** fundamentally answer:

> “What color is this triangle?”

That is shading.

It answers something closer to:

> “For this projected triangle, which sample locations lie inside it, and what interpolated primitive data should each generated fragment receive?”

The logical pipeline we are constructing is:

$$
\text{vertex/index memory}
\rightarrow
\text{primitive assembly}
\rightarrow
\text{vertex processing}
\rightarrow
\text{clip coordinates}
\rightarrow
\text{clipping}
\rightarrow
\text{perspective divide}
\rightarrow
\text{NDC}
\rightarrow
\text{viewport}
\rightarrow
\text{triangle setup}
\rightarrow
\text{coverage}
\rightarrow
\text{interpolation}
\rightarrow
\text{fragment invocation}
\rightarrow
\text{depth test}.
$$

Keep four words separate throughout this phase:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Pixel** | A discrete image location/storage location. |
| **Sample** | A point where coverage/depth may be evaluated. One pixel can have multiple samples. |
| **Fragment** | Candidate rasterized work generated from a primitive for one pixel/sample region. |
| **Framebuffer value** | The value eventually stored after tests/blending/etc. |

A fragment is therefore not automatically a final pixel.

---

**Parts 1802–1814 — what enters the graphics pipeline**

A vertex should be mentally understood as an **attribute record**, not as “a position.”

A useful CPU representation is:

```cpp
struct Vertex
{
    Vec3 position;   // Geometry, object/local space.
    Vec3 normal;     // Surface direction.
    Vec2 uv;         // Texture parameterization.
    Vec3 color;      // Optional authored data.
};
```

A GPU vertex fetch operation conceptually receives an index $i$ and reads fields such as

$$
\text{position}[i],\quad
\text{normal}[i],\quad
\text{uv}[i].
$$

The position is only one member of a vertex record.

This distinction becomes extremely important when vertices share a geometric location but require different attributes. A cube has eight geometric corner positions, but a hard-edged textured cube commonly needs more than eight rendering vertices because one corner can require several different normals or UV coordinates.

So:

$$
\text{geometric point} \neq \text{rendering vertex}.
$$

---

**Indexed geometry and why indices exist**

Consider two triangles making a quad:

$$
v_0=(-1,-1),\;
v_1=(1,-1),\;
v_2=(1,1),\;
v_3=(-1,1).
$$

Without indices:

```text
Triangle 0: v0 v1 v2
Triangle 1: v0 v2 v3
```

Six complete vertex records must be referenced.

With indexing:

```cpp
vertices = { v0, v1, v2, v3 };

indices = {
    0, 1, 2,
    0, 2, 3
};
```

Now four vertex records plus six small integer references describe the mesh.

This provides two different savings.

The obvious saving is **memory/bandwidth**: shared vertices do not need duplicate attribute records.

The subtler saving is **vertex shader work**.

Modern hardware normally contains a small cache of transformed vertices. If index $2$ was recently processed and appears again, the previous vertex shader result may be reused instead of invoking the vertex shader again.

Conceptually:

```text
index stream
0 1 2 0 2 3
    │   │
    └───┴─ recently transformed vertices may be reused
```

This is the **post-transform cache** idea from Part 1804.

It is important not to form the wrong abstraction:

> Indexed rendering does not promise “the vertex shader executes exactly once per unique index for the entire draw.”

Cache capacity is finite. Reuse depends on locality and implementation.

The practical mesh-optimization goal is therefore often to reorder triangles so recently used vertices are referenced again soon.

---

**Index formats**

Typical index widths are:

$$
16\text{-bit} \quad \text{or} \quad 32\text{-bit}.
$$

A 16-bit unsigned index can address

$$
2^{16}=65536
$$

possible vertex indices.

Its major advantage is bandwidth.

For $3\,000\,000$ indices:

$$
3\,000\,000\times2 = 6\text{ MB}
$$

versus

$$
3\,000\,000\times4 = 12\text{ MB}.
$$

The index stream is consumed heavily during rendering, so this is not necessarily trivial.

The downside is obviously the maximum vertex range per indexed region.

Your current Kairo implementation chooses the straightforward 32-bit path.

`KairoRenderer/Mesh.cppm`, current main:

```text
23–29   MeshVertex contains Position, Color, Normal, TexCoord
39–46   Mesh owns vector<MeshVertex> and vector<uint32_t>
61      IndexBytes = indexCount * sizeof(uint32_t)
```

and `VulkanTriangle.cppm` currently binds:

```cpp
vkCmdBindIndexBuffer(..., VK_INDEX_TYPE_UINT32);
vkCmdDrawIndexed(...);
```

at approximately lines **716–718** of the current file.

So this is a concrete instance of:

$$
\boxed{\text{theory: indexed geometry}
\rightarrow
\text{Kairo: uint32 index buffer}
\rightarrow
\text{Vulkan indexed draw}}
$$

---

**Primitive topology**

An index stream alone does not say how indices form primitives.

The **topology** supplies that interpretation.

For a triangle list,

```text
0 1 2 | 3 4 5 | 6 7 8
```

means three independent triangles.

For a strip,

```text
0 1 2 3 4
```

constructs overlapping triangles:

$$
(0,1,2),\quad
(1,2,3),\quad
(2,3,4)
$$

with winding conventions adjusted appropriately.

Triangle strips historically saved vertex/index bandwidth, but indexed triangle lists are generally simpler to construct, reorder, cull, batch and process in modern engines.

Kairo currently explicitly uses

```cpp
VK_PRIMITIVE_TOPOLOGY_TRIANGLE_LIST
```

when creating its mesh pipeline.

That corresponds directly to Parts 1805–1808.

---

**Primitive assembly**

Suppose the index buffer contains

```text
12 27 31
```

for a triangle-list draw.

Primitive assembly conceptually performs

$$
i_0=12,\quad i_1=27,\quad i_2=31
$$

and associates the outputs of those vertex shader invocations into one triangle.

Primitive assembly therefore bridges:

$$
\text{independent processed vertices}
\rightarrow
\text{topological primitives}.
$$

This matters because later operations—clipping, culling and rasterization—operate on the **primitive**, not isolated vertices.

---

**Vertex buffer layouts**

There are two major memory organizations.

An interleaved or Array-of-Structures representation is:

```text
Vertex 0: position normal uv color
Vertex 1: position normal uv color
Vertex 2: position normal uv color
...
```

or in C++:

```cpp
struct Vertex
{
    Vec3 position;
    Vec3 normal;
    Vec2 uv;
    Vec3 color;
};

std::vector<Vertex> vertices;
```

A separate-stream / Structure-of-Arrays style representation is:

```text
positions: P0 P1 P2 P3 ...
normals:   N0 N1 N2 N3 ...
uvs:       U0 U1 U2 U3 ...
colors:    C0 C1 C2 C3 ...
```

Neither is universally superior.

If every shader consumes every attribute, interleaving gives convenient spatial locality.

If one pass needs only positions—for example a shadow/depth pass—separate streams can avoid dragging normals, UVs and colors through memory.

Modern engines therefore often use several streams:

```text
stream 0: position
stream 1: normal + tangent + UV
stream 2: skin weights/joints
```

rather than dogmatically choosing pure AoS or pure SoA.

Your Kairo mesh path currently uses an interleaved base vertex stream.

The actual current Vulkan declaration is:

```cpp
meshBinding.binding   = 0;
meshBinding.stride    = sizeof(MeshVertex);
meshBinding.inputRate = VK_VERTEX_INPUT_RATE_VERTEX;
```

with locations:

```text
0 -> R32G32B32 position
1 -> R32G32B32 color
2 -> R32G32B32 normal
3 -> R32G32    UV
```

in `VulkanTriangle.cppm` lines approximately **447–458**.

There is a second vertex stream when skinning data exists.

That is a good real example of a hybrid layout.

---

**Vertex input formats are interpretation contracts**

A GPU buffer is fundamentally bytes.

Suppose memory contains:

```text
00 00 80 3F ...
```

Those bytes do not intrinsically mean “1.0.”

The pipeline vertex format tells hardware how to interpret them.

For example:

```cpp
VK_FORMAT_R32G32B32_SFLOAT
```

means:

```text
three consecutive 32-bit IEEE float components
```

whereas a packed normalized 8-bit format could mean:

```text
four 8-bit integers
mapped into [0,1]
```

before being exposed to the shader.

Therefore vertex input consists of at least:

$$
\boxed{\text{buffer}+\text{stride}+\text{offset}+\text{format}+\text{location}}
$$

A classic corruption bug occurs when these contracts disagree.

For example:

```cpp
struct Vertex
{
    Vec3 position;   // offset 0
    Vec3 normal;     // offset 12
    Vec2 uv;         // offset 24
};
```

but Vulkan is told

```text
normal offset = 16
```

Then the GPU faithfully reads incorrect bytes.

There is no semantic notion of “normal” at this stage. Hardware sees offsets and formats.

---

**Parts 1815–1818 — the coordinate-space chain**

Now we reach the central transformation spine.

For a local/object-space position

$$
\mathbf p_o=
\begin{pmatrix}
x\\y\\z\\1
\end{pmatrix},
$$

the conventional transformation is

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf p_c
=
PVM\mathbf p_o
}
$$

assuming column-vector notation.

The spaces are:

$$
\boxed{
\text{object}
\xrightarrow{M}
\text{world}
\xrightarrow{V}
\text{view}
\xrightarrow{P}
\text{clip}
}
$$

Do not collapse these into “MVP transforms the vertex.”

Each transition answers a different question.

---

### Object → world

$$
\mathbf p_w=M\mathbf p_o.
$$

The model matrix places one object's authored coordinates into the common world.

A chair model may have a vertex

$$
(0.3,1.0,-0.2)
$$

relative to the chair's own origin.

After the model transformation it might occupy

$$
(12.3,1.0,-8.2)
$$

in the scene.

---

### World → view

$$
\mathbf p_v=V\mathbf p_w.
$$

The view transformation expresses the world relative to the camera.

Rather than thinking:

> “The camera moved.”

The matrix interpretation is usually easier:

> “Transform the world into the camera's coordinate frame.”

---

### View → clip

$$
\mathbf p_c=P\mathbf p_v.
$$

The projection matrix does something more interesting than “make things smaller with distance.”

It creates a **homogeneous representation** in which later division by $w_c$ produces perspective.

The result is

$$
\mathbf p_c=
(x_c,y_c,z_c,w_c).
$$

This is **clip space**.

It is not NDC.

That distinction is absolutely essential.

---

**Your actual vertex shader**

Current `KairoRenderer/shaders/triangle.vert` performs:

```glsl
const vec4 worldPosition =
    draw.model * vec4(inPosition, 1.0);

gl_Position =
    camera.projection * camera.view * worldPosition;
```

lines approximately **40–41**.

Therefore the actual Kairo path is:

```text
MeshVertex.Position
        ↓
draw.model
        ↓
worldPosition
        ↓
camera.view
        ↓
view
        ↓
camera.projection
        ↓
gl_Position = clip coordinates
```

The shader also explicitly forwards:

```text
vertex color
normal
world-space position
light clip position
UV
```

to the fragment stage.

That will become critical when we discuss interpolation.

---

**Why clip coordinates have four components**

Perspective projection cannot be represented as a plain 3×3 Euclidean linear transform.

The trick of projective geometry is to delay division.

We construct something approximately of the form

$$
x_c = s_xx_v,
$$

$$
y_c = s_yy_v,
$$

and

$$
w_c \propto -z_v
$$

for the common right-handed camera convention.

Then

$$
x_{\text{ndc}}
=
\frac{x_c}{w_c}
\approx
\frac{s_xx_v}{-z_v}.
$$

So as distance increases, projected size decreases.

The perspective effect therefore occurs specifically because:

$$
\boxed{x_{\text{ndc}} = x_c/w_c}
$$

and similarly for $y$.

The projection matrix prepares the numerator and denominator.

The divide creates perspective.

---

**Why clipping must happen before perspective division**

This is one of the most important conceptual points in M109.

Consider a triangle crossing the camera/near plane.

One vertex may have a valid positive homogeneous $w$; another may approach

$$
w\rightarrow0.
$$

If you divide first,

$$
x/w
$$

can explode toward infinity.

A triangle that is geometrically ordinary in projective space turns into absurd screen coordinates.

Therefore the logical order is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{clip-space primitive}
\rightarrow
\text{homogeneous clipping}
\rightarrow
\text{perspective divide}
}
$$

not:

$$
\text{divide}
\rightarrow
\text{try to clip giant screen triangle}.
$$

The current Vulkan specification defines the usual clip volume as

$$
-w_c\le x_c\le w_c,
$$

$$
-w_c\le y_c\le w_c,
$$

$$
0\le z_c\le w_c
$$

unless the optional negative-one-to-one depth convention is enabled. [Khronos Registry](https://registry.khronos.org/vulkan/specs/latest-ratified/pdf/vkspec.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Notice that every inequality is expressed in terms of the homogeneous coordinate $w_c$.

That is why the stage is called **homogeneous clipping**.

---

**Clip planes as signed functions**

Each clipping boundary can be written as

$$
d(\mathbf v)\ge0.
$$

For example, the left plane

$$
x_c\ge-w_c
$$

becomes

$$
x_c+w_c\ge0.
$$

Define

$$
d_L(\mathbf v)=x_c+w_c.
$$

Similarly:

$$
d_R=w_c-x_c,
$$

$$
d_B=y_c+w_c,
$$

$$
d_T=w_c-y_c,
$$

$$
d_N=z_c,
$$

$$
d_F=w_c-z_c.
$$

Then a point is inside a particular plane when its corresponding $d$ is non-negative.

This unifies clipping into one operation.

---

**Clipping an edge against a plane**

Suppose edge endpoints are $A$ and $B$.

Their signed plane values are

$$
d_A=d(A),\qquad
d_B=d(B).
$$

The segment is

$$
P(t)=A+t(B-A),\quad t\in[0,1].
$$

Because a clip-plane function is linear,

$$
d(P(t))
=
d_A+t(d_B-d_A).
$$

At the intersection,

$$
d(P(t))=0.
$$

Therefore

$$
d_A+t(d_B-d_A)=0
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
t=
\frac{d_A}{d_A-d_B}
}.
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
P=A+t(B-A)
}.
$$

That formula is the entire mathematical core of polygon clipping against one linear half-space.

---

**Canonical clipping code**

```cpp
struct ClipVertex
{
    Vec4 position;     // x_c, y_c, z_c, w_c

    // These are outputs produced by the pre-rasterization stage.
    // When clipping introduces a new vertex, they must be interpolated
    // consistently along the original primitive edge.
    Vec3 worldPosition;
    Vec3 normal;
    Vec2 uv;
};

template<class PlaneDistance>
std::vector<ClipVertex> ClipAgainstPlane(
    std::span<const ClipVertex> input,
    PlaneDistance distance)
{
    std::vector<ClipVertex> output;

    if (input.empty())
        return output;

    ClipVertex previous = input.back();
    float dPrevious = distance(previous.position);
    bool previousInside = dPrevious >= 0.0f;

    for (const ClipVertex& current : input)
    {
        const float dCurrent = distance(current.position);
        const bool currentInside = dCurrent >= 0.0f;

        // Crossing the plane means one endpoint is inside and the
        // other is outside. Generate the intersection vertex.
        if (currentInside != previousInside)
        {
            const float denominator = dPrevious - dCurrent;

            // dPrevious / (dPrevious - dCurrent)
            // is obtained by solving d(A + t(B-A)) = 0.
            const float t = dPrevious / denominator;

            ClipVertex intersection;

            intersection.position =
                previous.position +
                t * (current.position - previous.position);

            intersection.worldPosition =
                previous.worldPosition +
                t * (current.worldPosition - previous.worldPosition);

            intersection.normal =
                previous.normal +
                t * (current.normal - previous.normal);

            intersection.uv =
                previous.uv +
                t * (current.uv - previous.uv);

            output.push_back(intersection);
        }

        if (currentInside)
            output.push_back(current);

        previous       = current;
        dPrevious      = dCurrent;
        previousInside = currentInside;
    }

    return output;
}
```

This is essentially Sutherland–Hodgman clipping applied in homogeneous space.

For a complete Vulkan-style view volume, apply six planes sequentially.

The output polygon may contain more than three vertices and is then triangulated.

---

**Perspective divide**

Once a primitive has survived clipping, its clip-space positions undergo:

$$
\boxed{
x_d=\frac{x_c}{w_c},\qquad
y_d=\frac{y_c}{w_c},\qquad
z_d=\frac{z_c}{w_c}
}
$$

where the subscript $d$ denotes normalized device coordinates.

This is the perspective divide defined by Vulkan's coordinate transformation stage. [Khronos Registry](https://registry.khronos.org/vulkan/specs/latest-ratified/pdf/vkspec.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Typical Vulkan NDC is

$$
x_d,y_d\in[-1,1]
$$

and

$$
z_d\in[0,1].
$$

Do not confuse that with traditional OpenGL's historical

$$
z\in[-1,1].
$$

This distinction becomes particularly important when building projection matrices.

---

**NDC is not screen space**

NDC is still resolution independent.

A vertex at

$$
(0,0)
$$

is the center regardless of whether the target is:

```text
800×600
1920×1080
3840×2160
```

The viewport transformation maps NDC into actual framebuffer coordinates.

For viewport width $W$, height $H$, origin $(x_0,y_0)$:

$$
x_f=x_0+\frac{W}{2}(x_d+1),
$$

$$
y_f=y_0+\frac{H}{2}(y_d+1)
$$

for a positive-height Vulkan viewport.

The formal Vulkan form is

$$
x_f=\frac{p_x}{2}x_d+o_x,
$$

$$
y_f=\frac{p_y}{2}y_d+o_y,
$$

$$
z_f=p_z z_d+o_z.
$$ :chatgpt-content-reference{index="4"}


---

**The Vulkan Y problem and what Kairo actually does**

Framebuffer $y$ normally grows downward.

Mathematical camera coordinates normally treat positive $y$ as upward.

There are several ways to reconcile that.

One is a negative Vulkan viewport height.

Another is modifying the projection matrix.

Your current `Camera.cppm` chooses the second strategy.

Current lines roughly 115–140:

```cpp
Mat4f projection = Perspective(...);

// Vulkan positive-height viewport.
// Flip clip-space Y once.
projection(1u, 1u) *= -1.0f;
```

That is a good example of why coordinate-space conventions must be traced rather than guessed.

Your pipeline is effectively:

```text
world Y-up
    ↓
view
    ↓
projection
    ↓
explicit clip-space Y flip
    ↓
positive-height Vulkan viewport
    ↓
framebuffer coordinates
```

If you later introduced a negative-height viewport without removing this projection flip, you would flip twice.

That is a classic “everything is upside down” bug.

---

**M110 begins — screen-space triangle setup**

After viewport transformation, suppose the projected triangle is

$$
v_0=(2,2),\quad
v_1=(8,3),\quad
v_2=(4,9).
$$

The rasterizer needs to answer:

> Which sample locations lie within this triangle?

It does not perform a point-in-polygon test from scratch for every sample.

Triangles admit an extremely efficient affine representation using **edge equations**.

---

**Edge functions**

For directed edge $a\rightarrow b$, define

$$
\boxed{
E_{ab}(p)
=
(b_x-a_x)(p_y-a_y)
-
(b_y-a_y)(p_x-a_x)
}
$$

This is a 2D cross product.

Geometrically,

$$
E_{ab}(p)
$$

is proportional to the signed area of the parallelogram formed by

$$
b-a
$$

and

$$
p-a.
$$

Its sign says which side of the directed line $p$ lies on.

It can be expanded into

$$
E(x,y)=Ax+By+C.
$$

Specifically,

$$
A=-(b_y-a_y),
$$

$$
B=b_x-a_x,
$$

$$
C=(b_y-a_y)a_x-(b_x-a_x)a_y.
$$

Now something wonderful happens.

Moving one pixel in $x$:

$$
E(x+1,y)=E(x,y)+A.
$$

Moving one pixel in $y$:

$$
E(x,y+1)=E(x,y)+B.
$$

So once an edge equation has been evaluated at one location, nearby samples can be evaluated through additions instead of recomputing everything.

This is why edge equations map beautifully to hardware rasterizers.

---

**Triangle orientation and signed area**

Take

$$
v_0,v_1,v_2.
$$

The doubled signed triangle area is

$$
\boxed{
A_2=E_{v_0v_1}(v_2)
}.
$$

If

$$
A_2>0
$$

under our chosen $y$-up convention, the vertices are counter-clockwise.

If

$$
A_2<0,
$$

they are clockwise.

If

$$
A_2=0,
$$

the triangle is degenerate.

Three points lie on one line.

No finite-area region exists to rasterize.

This same area quantity will shortly become the denominator of barycentric coordinates.

So one determinant drives:

$$
\text{orientation},
\quad
\text{degeneracy},
\quad
\text{coverage},
\quad
\text{barycentrics}.
$$

That is a very important unification.

---

**Inside-triangle tests**

Assume the triangle orientation has been normalized consistently.

A sample $p$ is inside when it lies on the interior side of all three edges.

Conceptually:

$$
E_{01}(p)\ge0,
$$

$$
E_{12}(p)\ge0,
$$

$$
E_{20}(p)\ge0.
$$

That gives a complete triangle point test.

The rasterizer therefore computes a bounding rectangle:

$$
x_{\min}=
\lfloor\min(x_0,x_1,x_2)\rfloor,
$$

etc.,

then only visits samples inside that box.

This converts a theoretical scan over the entire framebuffer into work approximately proportional to the triangle's screen footprint.

---

**Why `>= 0` is not sufficient**

Imagine two adjacent triangles sharing exactly one edge.

Triangle A says the shared edge belongs to it.

Triangle B also says the shared edge belongs to it.

Then shared-edge pixels can be shaded twice.

If instead both use a strict test,

$$
E>0,
$$

neither triangle owns the exact boundary.

Then cracks can appear.

Hardware therefore needs a deterministic ownership convention.

The common convention is the **top-left rule**.

Samples exactly on particular top/left boundary edges count as covered; samples exactly on the complementary bottom/right edges do not.

The crucial invariant is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{a shared edge is owned by exactly one adjacent triangle}
}
$$

rather than the wording “top” or “left” itself.

Hardware typically evaluates this using fixed-point/subpixel edge equations so neighboring primitives agree bit-for-bit about the shared edge.

This is one reason naive CPU rasterizers using arbitrary floating-point epsilons can disagree with GPU output at triangle boundaries.

---

**Pixel centers**

A pixel is an area.

Rasterization uses one or more **sample positions** within that area.

Under conventional single-sample rasterization, a logical pixel at integer coordinate

$$
(i,j)
$$

is normally tested at something equivalent to its center,

$$
(i+0.5,j+0.5).
$$

So asking whether pixel $(7,10)$ is covered does not usually mean evaluating the edge equations at

$$
(7,10).
$$

It means evaluating at the specified sample location inside that pixel.

That half-pixel detail is enough to generate visibly shifted rasterization when implemented incorrectly.

---

**MSAA sample positions**

With 4× MSAA, a pixel conceptually contains four coverage samples:

```text
+----------------+
|    •       •   |
|                |
|       pixel    |
|                |
| •          •   |
+----------------+
```

Their precise locations are implementation-defined or queryable depending on the graphics API/features.

Rasterization now produces a **coverage mask** such as

```text
sample 0 = covered
sample 1 = covered
sample 2 = not covered
sample 3 = covered
```

or binary

```text
1011
```

rather than a single yes/no pixel decision.

This is why MSAA improves geometric edge quality: coverage is measured more finely even if the fragment shader is not necessarily executed independently for every sample.

We will go much deeper into this in M111.

---

**Barycentric coordinates emerge directly from the same edge equations**

For triangle

$$
v_0,v_1,v_2
$$

and point $p$, define

$$
A=E_{12}(v_0).
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_0=
\frac{E_{12}(p)}{A}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_1=
\frac{E_{20}(p)}{A}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_2=
\frac{E_{01}(p)}{A}
}
$$

with

$$
\lambda_0+\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1.
$$

The geometry is beautiful.

Each numerator is the area of a subtriangle opposite one vertex.

Therefore at $v_0$:

$$
\lambda_0=1,\quad
\lambda_1=0,\quad
\lambda_2=0.
$$

At the centroid:

$$
\lambda_0=
\lambda_1=
\lambda_2=
\frac13.
$$

The same rasterization state has therefore simultaneously answered:

> Is this point inside?

and:

> Where inside the triangle is it?

---

**Affine attribute interpolation**

Suppose vertex colors are

$$
C_0=(1,0,0),
$$

$$
C_1=(0,1,0),
$$

$$
C_2=(0,0,1).
$$

For affine interpolation:

$$
\boxed{
C(p)=
\lambda_0C_0+
\lambda_1C_1+
\lambda_2C_2
}
$$

At the centroid:

$$
C=
\frac13(1,0,0)
+
\frac13(0,1,0)
+
\frac13(0,0,1)
$$

giving

$$
C=
\left(
\frac13,\frac13,\frac13
\right).
$$

That works perfectly when the quantity truly varies affinely in screen space.

But ordinary perspective-projected attributes do not.

This creates one of rasterization's most important traps.

---

**Why naive screen-space interpolation is wrong**

Imagine an edge in 3D with endpoints

$$
A,\qquad B
$$

at different depths.

A texture coordinate varies linearly along the actual 3D edge.

After perspective projection, however, equal intervals in world/view space do **not** become equal intervals on screen.

Perspective performs approximately

$$
x'=\frac{x}{z}.
$$

That division is nonlinear.

Therefore if you calculate screen barycentrics and directly perform

$$
u=
\lambda_0u_0+
\lambda_1u_1+
\lambda_2u_2,
$$

the result is generally not the texture coordinate corresponding to the original projected 3D point.

This causes the classic affine-texture “swimming” or warping seen in early software renderers and some older consoles.

---

**Deriving perspective-correct interpolation**

Let the original primitive-space barycentric weights be

$$
\alpha_i.
$$

A pre-projection varying $a$ satisfies

$$
a=
\sum_i\alpha_i a_i.
$$

After perspective division, the screen-space barycentrics become different values

$$
\lambda_i.
$$

The relationship is

$$
\alpha_i
=
\frac{\lambda_i/w_i}
{\sum_j\lambda_j/w_j}.
$$

Substitute that into the attribute equation:

$$
a=
\sum_i
a_i
\frac{\lambda_i/w_i}
{\sum_j\lambda_j/w_j}.
$$

The denominator is shared:

$$
\boxed{
a(p)
=
\frac{
\displaystyle
\sum_i\lambda_i\frac{a_i}{w_i}
}{
\displaystyle
\sum_i\lambda_i\frac1{w_i}
}
}
$$

This is the perspective-correct interpolation equation.

The implementation interpretation is even more important than memorizing it.

At every vertex, think of storing:

$$
\frac{a_i}{w_i}
$$

and

$$
\frac1{w_i}.
$$

Rasterization linearly interpolates those screen-space quantities.

Then reconstruct:

$$
a=
\frac{a/w}{1/w}.
$$

So:

$$
\boxed{
\text{interpolate reciprocal }w
}
$$

is not some random graphics trick.

It is what mathematically undoes the projective distortion introduced by dividing coordinates by $w$.

---

**A numerical example**

Suppose two endpoints have

$$
u_0=0,\qquad w_0=1
$$

and

$$
u_1=1,\qquad w_1=4.
$$

At the screen midpoint,

$$
\lambda_0=\lambda_1=0.5.
$$

Naive interpolation gives

$$
u_{\text{naive}}
=
0.5(0)+0.5(1)=0.5.
$$

Perspective-correct interpolation instead computes

$$
\frac{u_0}{w_0}=0,
$$

$$
\frac{u_1}{w_1}=0.25,
$$

and

$$
\frac1{w_0}=1,\qquad
\frac1{w_1}=0.25.
$$

Therefore

$$
u=
\frac{
0.5(0)+0.5(0.25)
}{
0.5(1)+0.5(0.25)
}
$$

$$
=
\frac{0.125}{0.625}
$$

$$
=
0.2.
$$

Not

$$
0.5.
$$

That is a massive difference.

The nearer endpoint occupies more of the apparent screen-space perspective relationship.

---

**Canonical interpolation code**

```cpp
template<typename T>
T PerspectiveInterpolate(
    const T& a0,
    const T& a1,
    const T& a2,
    float w0,
    float w1,
    float w2,
    float lambda0,
    float lambda1,
    float lambda2)
{
    // Interpolate reciprocal homogeneous W.
    const float reciprocalW =
        lambda0 / w0 +
        lambda1 / w1 +
        lambda2 / w2;

    // Interpolate attribute/W in screen space.
    const T numerator =
        a0 * (lambda0 / w0) +
        a1 * (lambda1 / w1) +
        a2 * (lambda2 / w2);

    // Recover the original varying.
    return numerator / reciprocalW;
}
```

That one function connects Parts 1832–1835.

---

**`smooth`, `noperspective`, and `flat`**

There are conceptually three useful interpolation behaviors.

The normal perspective mode is equivalent to:

```glsl
smooth
```

and uses the equation we derived.

`noperspective` instead performs plain framebuffer-space interpolation:

$$
a=
\lambda_0a_0+
\lambda_1a_1+
\lambda_2a_2.
$$

That can be desirable for screen-space quantities.

`flat` performs no interpolation at all. One provoking vertex supplies the primitive's value.

Integer varyings are generally flat because interpolating discrete IDs such as

```text
material ID = 17
object ID = 42
```

would make no semantic sense.

---

**Fragment shader invocation**

Once a covered location survives enough rasterization setup, the implementation can generate a fragment shader invocation.

Conceptually the shader receives interpolated inputs:

```glsl
layout(location=0) in vec3 inColor;
layout(location=1) in vec3 inNormal;
layout(location=2) in vec3 inWorldPosition;
layout(location=3) in vec4 inLightClipPosition;
layout(location=4) in vec2 inTexCoord;
```

That is exactly the current `triangle.frag` interface in your Kairo renderer.

The fragment shader does **not** receive the three original vertices.

The rasterizer has already transformed those per-vertex outputs into per-fragment interpolated values.

That distinction separates the pre-rasterization and post-rasterization stages.

---

**Screen-space derivatives**

Now consider:

```glsl
dFdx(value)
dFdy(value)
```

These are not symbolic calculus operations performed by a compiler.

The GPU executes fragment work in small neighboring groups—traditionally reasoned about as $2\times2$ quads.

Suppose a varying $f$ has values approximately

```text
f00    f10

f01    f11
```

Then a horizontal derivative can be approximated through neighboring invocation differences such as

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}
\approx
f_{10}-f_{00},
$$

and vertically,

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}
\approx
f_{01}-f_{00}.
$$

Vulkan/SPIR-V formally defines fine/coarse derivative behavior over derivative groups/quads; ordinary derivative instructions may use an implementation-selected fine or coarse form. Implicit-LOD texture sampling itself relies on coordinate derivatives. [Khronos Registry](https://registry.khronos.org/vulkan/specs/latest/pdf/vkspec.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

This is why fragments outside the actual primitive can sometimes exist as **helper invocations**: a neighboring live fragment may need their values to calculate derivatives.

They participate in computation but must not produce ordinary framebuffer side effects.

---

**What your Kairo fragment shader actually uses derivatives for**

This is one of the strongest repository mappings in this pass.

Current `triangle.frag`, lines approximately **121–136**:

```glsl
const vec3 geometricNormal = normalize(inNormal);

const vec3 dpdx = dFdx(inWorldPosition);
const vec3 dpdy = dFdy(inWorldPosition);

const vec2 duvdx = dFdx(inTexCoord);
const vec2 duvdy = dFdy(inTexCoord);

const float determinant =
    duvdx.x * duvdy.y -
    duvdx.y * duvdy.x;
```

Then it reconstructs a tangent:

```glsl
tangent =
    (dpdx * duvdy.y -
     dpdy * duvdx.y) /
    determinant;
```

This is solving the local differential system

$$
dP
=
T\,du+B\,dv.
$$

Across screen $x$:

$$
P_x
=
T\,u_x+B\,v_x
$$

and across screen $y$:

$$
P_y
=
T\,u_y+B\,v_y.
$$

Write this as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
P_x & P_y
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
T & B
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
u_x & u_y\\
v_x & v_y
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The UV Jacobian determinant is

$$
D=u_xv_y-u_yv_x.
$$

Solving gives

$$
\boxed{
T=
\frac{
P_xv_y-P_yv_x
}{D}
}
$$

which is exactly what your shader implements.

It checks

$$
|D|>10^{-8}
$$

before dividing.

So the code is not merely “using dFdx for normal maps.”

It is solving a local $2\times2$ coordinate transformation between screen-space variation and texture-space variation.

That is the math-to-code bridge your curriculum is asking for.

---

**Derivative failure cases**

If UVs collapse locally,

$$
D\approx0,
$$

the tangent basis becomes singular.

Examples include degenerate UV triangles, duplicated UV coordinates and extremely compressed texture parameterization.

Then

$$
1/D
$$

becomes enormous and the tangent can explode numerically.

Your shader handles this by leaving the geometric normal in place when

$$
|D|\le10^{-8}.
$$

There is another important failure mode: derivatives inside highly divergent control flow.

If neighboring invocations do not execute compatible paths, derivative availability and meaning become tricky. Shader languages and APIs impose specific derivative-group rules; this is why derivative-based operations should not be casually hidden behind arbitrary per-fragment branches.

---

**Depth testing — what problem it solves**

Suppose two triangles project onto the same sample.

Triangle A produced depth

$$
z_A=0.3.
$$

Triangle B produced

$$
z_B=0.7.
$$

Under conventional Vulkan depth where smaller values are closer, A should win.

The depth buffer stores visibility history.

Conceptually:

```cpp
if (incomingDepth < storedDepth)
{
    storedDepth = incomingDepth;
    writeColor();
}
```

Without a depth buffer, visibility would depend almost entirely on draw order.

---

**Depth buffer representation**

Your current Kairo implementation uses

```cpp
VK_FORMAT_D32_SFLOAT
```

in `VulkanDepth.cppm`.

So each depth sample has a 32-bit floating-point depth component.

The image is created with

```cpp
VK_IMAGE_USAGE_DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT_BIT
```

and resides in device-local memory.

Current `VulkanTriangle` rendering clears depth to:

```cpp
depthClear.depthStencil = { 1.0f, 0u };
```

and uses viewport:

```cpp
minDepth = 0.0f;
maxDepth = 1.0f;
```

The pipeline currently performs:

```cpp
depth.depthTestEnable  = VK_TRUE;
depth.depthWriteEnable = VK_TRUE;
depth.depthCompareOp   = VK_COMPARE_OP_LESS;
```

around current lines **541–545**.

Therefore Kairo currently means:

```text
nearer → smaller depth
farther → larger depth

clear = 1
accept incoming if incoming < stored
```

That is conventional depth, not reversed-Z.

---

**Depth comparison functions**

Common comparisons conceptually include

```text
NEVER
LESS
EQUAL
LESS_OR_EQUAL
GREATER
NOT_EQUAL
GREATER_OR_EQUAL
ALWAYS
```

The choice is not cosmetic.

For conventional Z:

$$
\text{clear}=1,\qquad
\text{compare}=LESS
$$

is typical.

For reversed-Z:

$$
\text{clear}=0,\qquad
\text{compare}=GREATER
$$

or `GREATER_OR_EQUAL` is typical.

If you reverse the projection but forget the comparison function, almost everything disappears.

If you reverse the compare function but forget to change the clear value, nearly everything also disappears.

These parameters form one invariant.

---

**Depth write control**

Depth **testing** and depth **writing** are separate.

Opaque rendering normally uses:

```text
depth test  = enabled
depth write = enabled
```

because the nearest opaque surface should occlude later geometry.

Transparent rendering commonly uses:

```text
depth test  = enabled
depth write = disabled
```

because transparent fragments should generally be tested against opaque geometry without making the first transparent surface permanently hide every transparent layer behind it.

Your Kairo pipeline already reflects this distinction.

Its opaque pipeline is created with depth writes enabled, while the transparent path requests depth writes disabled.

That becomes important in Pass 2 when we cover transparency ordering.

---

**Early versus late depth testing**

The conceptual pipeline might be drawn:

```text
rasterize
  ↓
fragment shader
  ↓
depth test
```

but that can waste enormous work.

Suppose an expensive fragment shader executes 200 instructions and the resulting fragment is completely hidden behind existing geometry.

If the GPU already knows its depth will fail, it would prefer:

```text
rasterize
  ↓
depth test
  ↓
if visible → execute shader
```

That is **early depth testing**.

Vulkan explicitly models early-fragment-test and late-fragment-test pipeline stages: early tests occur before fragment shading, late tests after it. [Khronos Registry](https://registry.khronos.org/VulkanSC/specs/1.0-extensions/man/html/VkPipelineStageFlagBits2KHR.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

But whether an implementation can perform the optimization depends on shader behavior.

Things such as writing fragment depth, certain side effects, sample-mask manipulation or discard behavior can constrain what may safely happen early.

Your current Kairo fragment shader performs:

```glsl
if (alphaMask && alpha < cutoff)
    discard;
```

so you should not imagine the implementation as a simplistic immutable stage diagram.

Real GPUs often separate:

```text
early rejection
fragment execution
late/commit tests
```

and use hierarchical visibility optimizations around them.

---

**Why perspective depth is nonlinear**

This is the foundation of Parts 1844–1845.

Let positive camera distance be

$$
d=-z_v>0.
$$
